newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA COMMUNIST-ERA VICTIMS ON SWISS BANKS LIST.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA COMMUNIST-ERA VICTIMS ON SWISS BANKS LIST.

text.p: Publication of a list of dormant World War Two Swiss bank accounts has revived bitter memories of the Nazi Holocaust worldwide, but in Bulgaria it has also awakened memories of the communist atrocities that followed.

Georgi Rashkov, one of 12 Bulgarians on the list of some 1,800 account holders, was a member of parliament, wealthy businessman and philanthropist who became a victim of communist show trials and died in poverty.

His only heir is his daughter, pensioner Ana Basarska, who last winter was one of the thousands of elderly Bulgarians who qualified for a European Union cash handout to help them pay for food and heating, state radio reported.

Rashkov was one of 11,000 people tried by the People's Court set up after the communist takeover in Bulgaria in 1944 to try people for "involving the state in World War Two against the Allied Powers and for related crimes".
Rashkov was tried on March 13, 1945, by the Regional People's Court in his northern home town of Razgrad, records of the Chief Archives Directorate showed.
He was found guilty of embezzling municipality property and misuse of power and was sentenced to five years of confinement.
Rashkov, a deputy in the last Bulgarian pre-communist parliament and one of the wealthiest men in Razgrad, is still remembered for his philanthropy.

State radio said he had funded the paving of streets in the town, the building of a theatre and the upgrading of the water supply system, as well as giving financial support to local students and built a tourist rest-house near the town.

He owned a successful company exporting poultry, eggs and other agricultural products to Germany, Italy, Britain and the Middle East. His company, home and property were confiscated by the communist authorities, the radio said.

After the collapse of communist rule in 1989, the new authorities launched a restitution process which is still not complete. Under a bill passed by parliament in February 1992, the state should give back houses, flats, shop and factory space and other facilities seized between 1947 and 1952.
Rashkov died in 1962 -- unemployed, in a rented flat and with no income, said the radio.

Denko Sotirov, a former Bulgarian diplomat who fled the communist state in 1947 and now lives in London, told Reuters by telephone he had identified two other victims of the People's Courts among the Bulgarian account holders listed.

"Nikola Minkov, a deputy in the last parliament before 1944, and Petko Petkov, a leading public figure at that time, were sentenced by the People's Court, as all leading pre-communist political and public figures were," he said.
"Some of them managed to save their lives, but most were sentenced to death," he said.

In August last year the Supreme Court overturned death sentences or long jail terms against 48 pre-communist rulers and three royal regents imposed by the People's Court for their responsibility for the association with Germany during the war.

Among those executed were the last three prime ministers before the communist takeover -- Dobri Bozhilov, Ivan Bagryanov and Konstantin Mouraviev, and the brother of late King Boris, Prince Kiril, who was then a regent.

There were no Jewish names among the 12 Bulgarians in the Swiss banks' list. The wartime government saved Bulgaria's 50,000 Jews from deportation, refusing to hand them to the Nazis in 1943 despite its military alliance with Germany.
